implementation_notes: Default Ruby realization where Kafka is the broker: Karafka owns the consumer group, the offset commits and the rebalance handling, so the application only declares topics and checkpoints progress. Choose it when Rails-style apps consume an existing Kafka log.
code_sketch:
class EventsConsumer < ApplicationConsumer
  def consume
    messages.each { |m| handle(m.payload); mark_as_consumed(m) }
  end
end
pitfalls: mark_as_consumed only affects the next commit; a crash before the commit replays the batch.
Karafka's automatic commits can advance past buffered-but-unflushed work unless manual offset management is enabled.

variants.name: Bunny/AMQP durable queue bound to a durable exchange
variants.idiom_name: Bunny queue(durable: true) + queue.bind(durable exchange) + subscribe(block: true)
variants.implementation_notes: Where RabbitMQ is the broker, the queue itself is the retained backlog: messages stay in the durable queue while no consumer is attached, and bindings between durable queues and durable exchanges survive a broker restart. Choose it for work-queue style backlogs that are replayed to a single consumer group rather than per-subscriber.
variants.code_sketch:
conn = Bunny.new; conn.start
ch = conn.create_channel
exchange = ch.direct('orders', durable: true)
queue = ch.quorum_queue('billing-ledger')
queue.bind(exchange, routing_key: 'order.created')
queue.subscribe(block: true) { |info, props, body| handle(body) }
pitfalls: Queue-level retention is shared by competing consumers: this is the point-to-point mapping of the pattern, not per-subscriber fan-out.
A queue declared with different durability/arguments fails the declaration at runtime; TTL and max-length policies silently discard the oldest backlog.
